_comment: Registration for scripts/check-cpp-host-writes.py (issue #1132).
WHY THIS GATE NEEDS A COMMITTED CASE (ADR 0008): it lets work THROUGH.
`make verify` and the CI step read its green as 'every host write in the two
cpp command documents goes through the seam', and nothing downstream
re-derives it. A blind version reports the same clean line over the
half-seamed state #1139 shipped, where a defer-set naming ~/.bashrc refused
two writes, printed a stated refusal, and wrote the file anyway.
FOUR WRITE FORMS, ONE CASE EACH, because every enumeration BY SURFACE in
this issue missed something and the forms are what the gate actually reads.
THE FIFTH AND SIXTH CASES TEST THE FILTER ITSELF. A comment filter is not a
neutral refinement - it is a new way to be blind, so it needs both
directions: a comment must not red, and a write that merely LOOKS like one
must. Without the sixth, the obvious `"#" in line` implementation passes
every other case in this register.
POPULATION: the gate scans two documents and says so in its verdict. It
claims nothing about the other command families, which are not in its input.
Stdlib-only and git-free, like the gate: nothing here is absent from the
slim CI image, so the control gives the same verdict there as here.
A CASE THAT WAS WRITTEN AND THEN REMOVED: `bad-same-line-redirect`. The
anchor CATCHES it, because a same-line redirect is the one form the first
framing did implement, so the case cannot distinguish the gate from the
blind version. A case whose expected answer BOTH sides produce demonstrates
nothing about the difference between them - the same trap that nearly
shipped in #1139's control. The form is still exercised on every run, by the
real documents.
SECOND PROPERTY, ADDED BY #1198: the seam's VERDICT must be read. #1132
made every host write go through one door and nobody checked that the
door could be opened, or that its answer was listened to. The seam
returns 0 wrote / 3 deferred-by-request / 1 failed, plus 127 when it is
not installed - and all twenty call sites in the two documents discarded
it, so a checkmark was printed for all four.
Measured 2026-09-22: /cpp:update printed 'Flow allowlist merged (52 total
allow rules)' with the surface DEFERRED exactly as asked, and 'merged (2
total allow rules)' - the PRE-merge count - with the seam absent.
NO NEW ANCHOR IS NEEDED, and that is a finding rather than a shortcut. The
battery's contract is that an anchor must MISS every committed bad case -
it marks the control INERT otherwise, correctly, since an anchor stands for
the version the gate replaced. `first-framing` already satisfies that for
all seven: it misses the four #1132 forms AND the three #1198 ones, having
no unread-verdict check at all.
Three OTHER wrong implementations are committed under alternatives/ and
driven by tests/test_cpp_host_writes.py, because none of them is blind in
the battery's sense and registering one was MEASURED to report 'anchor
constructed CAUGHT the known-bad input':
- pre-1198 is the full previous gate, so it catches the four #1132 cases
- naive-next-line is PARTIALLY blind: it catches the claim-shaped case
and misses the silent loop and the heredoc-data one
- over-broad is the opposite error: it catches every bad case and reds on
the FIX, which is what the good- cases separate the gate from
committed bad case' - it marks the control INERT if an anchor catches one,
which is correct: an anchor is the version the gate replaced. Only pre-1198
meets that here. Two other wrong implementations are committed under
alternatives/ and driven by the test instead: naive-next-line is PARTIALLY
blind (it catches the claim-shaped case, misses the silent loop and heredoc
data) and over-broad is the opposite error (it catches every bad case and
reds on the fix). Registering either as an anchor was measured to produce
'anchor constructed CAUGHT the known-bad input'.
each excuses a different case. pre-1198 is the gate as it shipped and
misses every bad case. naive keys on a nearby checkmark and reads the raw
next LINE, so it excuses the silent loop and a $? that is heredoc data.
over-broad flags every seam invocation, passes every bad case, and reds on
the FIX - which is why the good- cases are load-bearing rather than
decorative. A gate that cannot be satisfied is a gate that gets removed.
FIVE CASES ADDED AFTER COUNTER-MODEL REVIEW OF THIS ISSUE'S OWN FIX. Every
one of them was a REPRODUCED defect in the first implementation of the
unread-verdict check, not a hazard someone imagined - which is why the
alternative they discriminate against, alternatives/proximity-framing, is
recovered from the index rather than constructed. The sharpest:
bad-quoted-invocation-unguarded. #1198's own bootstrap is a QUOTED
invocation, the first pattern required whitespace immediately after the
.sh, and a closing quote sits exactly there - so the gate could not see the
calls its fix had just added, and removing their handlers still read clean.
A gate blind to its own remedy is the failure this whole issue is about,
committed once inside the instrument built to catch it.
A SECOND COUNTER-MODEL PASS PRODUCED FIVE MORE CASES, and the reason is
worth more than the cases: the FIX for the first pass's false positive
introduced a false NEGATIVE. Requiring the seam at the head of the logical
line stopped it flagging prose, and stopped it seeing `true && echo ready;
<seam call>` entirely. Three implementations of one check now exist - all
three committed, two under alternatives/ - and each corrected its
predecessor while being wrong in a new way. That progression is the only
evidence the third is better rather than merely newer.
The third framing decides PER COMMAND rather than per line, because the
command is the thing that actually has an exit status - which is what the
whole issue is about.

cases.name: bad-indirect-shell
cases.why: The target is assigned $HOME on one line and written eight lines later. This is the shape that hid two ~/.bashrc writes through #1139 and a review: the verb and the path never share a line, so every same-line survey reported the file clean.

cases.name: bad-embedded-python
cases.why: A write_text() inside a python heredoc. Satisfies no grep for a redirect, cp, tee, mv or ln, which is why ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json was absent from three successive enumerations.

cases.name: bad-mkdir
cases.why: mkdir -p of a host directory. A directory is a surface: a defer-set naming ~/.claude must refuse its creation, not fall through to a permission error.

cases.name: bad-hash-inside-a-string
cases.why: THE FILTER'S OWN BAD CASE. printf '# managed by cpp' >> "$RC" is a real write whose line contains a hash inside a string. A comment filter written as `"#" in line` - the obvious first version - excuses it, and a block appended to a shell rc almost always carries exactly such a banner. The filter added to remove false positives is a new way to be blind, and this is the direction nobody re-checks.

cases.name: good-writes-only-in-comments
cases.why: Every write FORM present, each inside a real comment, plus one harmless echo. Three false positives in this issue's own analysis came from quoting a write in prose, so the filter must exist; this case is what stops it being removed, and it is byte-adjacent to the bad case above so the pair isolates the filter's rule rather than its existence.

cases.name: bad-unguarded-seam-call
cases.why: The measured shape: settings-merge followed by an unconditional checkmark. Discriminates against pre-1198, which has no unread-verdict check at all.

cases.name: bad-unguarded-loop-no-claim
cases.why: A link-into loop that claims nothing. This is what actually bit on 2026-09-22 - ninety calls, 25 scripts left unlinked, and the step reported no verdict either way. Discriminates against naive, which keys the finding on a nearby success claim and therefore excuses exactly this.

cases.name: bad-status-only-inside-heredoc
cases.why: `$?` appears on the line immediately after the seam call, inside a <<'JQ' body, where it is jq program text and not a handler. Discriminates against naive, which reads the raw next line and is satisfied by data.

cases.name: good-guarded-seam-call
cases.why: The fix shape - `case $?` naming wrote/deferred/failed. Discriminates against over-broad, which reds on every seam invocation and so cannot be satisfied by correcting the defect.

cases.name: good-seam-call-chained
cases.why: `|| handler` consults the status without a `case`. Keeps the check reading shell FORMS rather than one blessed spelling; discriminates against over-broad.

cases.name: good-continuation-then-handler
cases.why: A backslash continuation puts the statement's own ARGUMENTS on the following line and the handler after that. Discriminates against naive, which reports this correct code as unguarded - a false positive on the fix, which is the direction of error that gets a gate switched off.

cases.name: bad-quoted-invocation-unguarded
cases.why: A QUOTED invocation - "$CPP_DIR/.../cpp-host-write.sh" link-into - with no handler. This is the shape #1198's own bootstrap uses, and the first implementation of this gate could not see it: a closing quote sits where the pattern wanted whitespace, so deleting the bootstrap's handlers still produced a clean verdict. The gate was blind to its own fix. Discriminates against alternatives/proximity-framing.

cases.name: bad-neighbour-command-status
cases.why: `<seam call>` then `echo done; rc=$?`. `rc` holds ECHO's status, not the seam's, so the answer was discarded - and the first implementation accepted it, which is this issue's own defect living inside its detector. Discriminates against alternatives/proximity-framing.

cases.name: good-seam-named-in-prose
cases.why: An `echo` that NAMES the helper without invoking it. The first implementation reported it as an unread verdict; a gate that reds on its own documentation gets deleted rather than fixed. Discriminates against alternatives/proximity-framing.

cases.name: good-blank-line-before-handler
cases.why: A blank line between the call and its `case $?`. Ordinary formatting, reported as unguarded by the first implementation - a false positive on the FIX itself. Discriminates against alternatives/proximity-framing.

cases.name: good-same-line-status-capture
cases.why: `<seam call>; rc=$?` - the handler on the invocation's own statement, after a `;`. A legitimate spelling the first implementation called unguarded. Discriminates against alternatives/proximity-framing.

cases.name: bad-invocation-after-separator
cases.why: `true && echo ready; <seam call>` with an unconditional success message. The LINE-HEAD framing could not see the invocation at all - its fix for a false positive had created a false negative. Discriminates against alternatives/line-head-framing.

cases.name: bad-neighbour-chain-after-semicolon
cases.why: `<seam>; echo done && echo ready`. The `&&` reads ECHO's status, not the seam's, but a chain searched anywhere after the invocation accepted it. Discriminates against alternatives/line-head-framing.

cases.name: bad-status-captured-after-another-command
cases.why: `<seam>` then `true && rc=$?`. `rc` holds `true`'s status; the seam's answer was discarded. Discriminates against alternatives/line-head-framing.

cases.name: good-neighbouring-script-not-the-seam
cases.why: `./not-cpp-host-write.sh settings-merge` - a NEIGHBOUR's script. The path pattern accepted any prefix, so a finding named our seam for somebody else's command: a non-zero that cannot tell our thing from a neighbour's. Discriminates against alternatives/line-head-framing.

cases.name: good-seam-path-as-assignment-value
cases.why: `SEAM=<path> settings-merge` - an environment assignment whose executed command is `settings-merge`; the seam path is a VALUE, not the command. Discriminates against alternatives/line-head-framing.

anchors.note: Constructed, so --verify-provenance reports unverified, which is correct and must never be read as ok.
anchors.why: The framing this issue actually started from: grep for a redirect to a $HOME path, and treat any line containing a hash as a comment. It misses all four bad cases and each was a real miss before it was a fixture - the indirect form hid two ~/.bashrc writes through #1139 and a review, embedded python hid opencode.json from three enumerations, mkdir was never counted as a surface, and the naive filter excuses a banner line. It agrees on the good case, which is what keeps the demonstration isolated.
